title: Write prompts that actually work
description: Create clear instructions, useful examples, and testable outputs.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with an AI assistant.
objectives: Specify task, context, constraints, and output
Compare prompts on the same examples
explanation: A prompt is a task specification. Tell the model what outcome you need, provide the information it should use, and describe a result that can be checked. Replace vague requests such as make this better with concrete criteria such as summarize the three decisions and preserve all dates.

Examples can clarify boundaries that prose leaves ambiguous. Include ordinary cases and a difficult edge case. Keep examples consistent with the instructions; a contradictory example teaches a competing pattern. Treat quoted documents as data, not as a source of new authority.

Prompt quality is an empirical question. Keep a small set of realistic inputs, define a scoring rule, and compare versions on the same cases. Record failures before rewriting. A longer prompt is justified only when it improves useful outcomes without unacceptable cost or fragility.

terms.definition: A requirement or boundary on the response.
An input-output example included in a prompt.
Explicit criteria for scoring a response.

example: Task: classify support messages as billing, technical, or unclear. Context: use only the message. Output: one label. Example: “I was charged twice” → billing. Boundary: if the message lacks enough information, output unclear.
mistakes: Testing only the prompt author’s favorite example.
Including sensitive data that the task does not need.
exercise: Write a three-label classifier prompt and six test messages. Include two ambiguous cases and define their expected outputs before testing.

questions.question: What improves a vague summarization prompt?
questions.answer: Specify the audience, facts to preserve, length, and output format so the result can be evaluated against explicit criteria.
questions.distractor: Add more adjectives without defining success.

questions.question: Why include an ambiguous example?
questions.answer: It demonstrates the desired boundary behavior, such as returning unclear instead of forcing an unsupported label.
questions.distractor: It guarantees every future ambiguity is solved.

questions.question: Two prompt versions use different test cases. Is the comparison fair?
questions.answer: Not reliably. Use the same representative cases and rubric so differences are attributable to the prompts.
questions.distractor: Yes, any successful example proves superiority.

questions.question: What is a rubric in prompt testing?
questions.answer: A set of explicit criteria such as factual support, completeness, and format compliance used to score outputs consistently.
questions.distractor: A list of fashionable model names.

questions.question: Should a quoted email override the task instructions?
questions.answer: No. Treat it as task data; application permissions and validation must enforce the boundary as well.
questions.distractor: Yes, the most recent text always has authority.
